triage.name: Cold Sores
triage.reason: Common recognizable mucocutaneous infection with a straightforward history and exam diagnosis; good for primary care.

demographics: Most adults in the US carry HSV-1; many never have symptoms
Recurrent outbreaks are common in otherwise healthy people
First symptomatic infection is often in childhood or young adulthood

risk_factors.text: Prior HSV-1 infection (most adults are seropositive)
Close contact with someone who has an active cold sore (kissing, sharing utensils, towels)
Sun exposure or wind to the lips
Recent dental work or lip trauma

comorbidities: Atopic dermatitis (higher risk of eczema herpeticum)
social_history: Sharing drinks, utensils, or lip balm with others
exposures: Contact with a person who has an active cold sore

chief_complaints.text: I get a tingling bump on my lip that turns into a sore
My lip is burning and it hurts
I have a blister on my mouth

hpi.onset: Often begins with tingling, itching, or burning at the lip for a few hours to a day before a bump appears; first-ever episode may start with fever and mouth pain
hpi.duration: Sores crust and heal over 7–14 days; first episode may last up to 2–3 weeks
hpi.progression: Tingling or burning, then a small cluster of fluid-filled blisters, then crusting and healing without a scar
hpi.location: Usually on or around the outer lip, sometimes at the corner of the mouth or the nostril; inside the mouth on the gums or hard palate in a first episode
hpi.quality: Tender, burning, or stinging; the blisters are painful to touch
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; uncomfortable but not disabling
hpi.timing: Recurrent episodes can be triggered by sun, stress, fever, or menstruation; each episode runs its course over about 1–2 weeks
aggravating: Touching or picking at the sore
relieving: Lip balm or sunscreen lip protection

associated_symptoms.text: Tingling or burning before the sore appears
Tender or swollen lymph nodes under the jaw
Sore throat or swollen gums during a first episode
Drooling or refusing to eat in young children

pertinent_negatives: Sores only inside the mouth without lip involvement
Sores that have not healed after 3 weeks

positives.text: Low-grade fever with a first episode
Sore on the lip or around the mouth
Sore throat or gum pain with a first episode

argues_against: Deep ulceration of the palate or tonsils

positives.text: Cluster of small blisters on the lip
Crusted sore at the lip margin

negatives: Rash on the trunk or extremities

positives.text: Mouth pain that makes eating uncomfortable

atypical.how_it_differs: A first infection often causes fever, irritability, swollen gums, many mouth ulcers, drooling, and refusal to eat; the child may not be able to describe tingling.
Sores can be larger, more numerous, slower to heal, and may spread to other skin areas or inside the mouth.
missing_classic_features: Small, self-limited sore that heals in 1–2 weeks

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with fever, poor feeding, and irritability rather than a clear lip sore; neonatal infection is a serious concern and needs urgent care.
May have more frequent or slower-healing outbreaks, and other causes of mouth sores such as medication reactions or nutritional deficiencies are more likely.

general.moderate: Well-appearing but uncomfortable when the sore is touched or when eating
general.severe: Ill-appearing with fever and mouth pain, reluctant to eat or drink
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, dehydrated, lethargic (consider disseminated HSV or another diagnosis)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, mouth corners, and nostrils in good light
findings.finding: Cluster of small, thin-walled, fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base at the vermilion border of the lip

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips and perioral skin
findings.finding: Crusted or ulcerated lesion at the lip margin (later stage of the same outbreak)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lip where the patient reports tingling
findings.finding: Localized erythema or swelling before vesicles appear

findings.maneuver: Gently palpate the lesion (or ask about tenderness rather than pressing hard)
Inspect the gums, buccal mucosa, tongue, and hard palate
findings.finding: Multiple shallow ulcers on the gingiva or hard palate (typical of a first episode, primary gingivostomatitis)

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently palpate the gums
findings.finding: Swollen, erythematous gingiva that bleeds easily

findings.maneuver: Palpate the submandibular and cervical lymph node chains
findings.finding: Tender, enlarged submandibular or anterior cervical lymph nodes

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctivae and ask about eye pain, redness, or blurred vision
findings.finding: No conjunctival injection, no corneal lesion, no eye pain or discharge

findings.maneuver: Assess mental status and, if symptoms suggest it, check for neck stiffness and focal deficits
findings.finding: Alert and oriented, no neck stiffness, no focal neurologic deficit

findings.maneuver: Inspect the trunk, back, and extremities
findings.finding: No widespread vesicular or dermatomal rash

findings.maneuver: Ask about genital sores; examine only if symptoms are reported
Assess mucous membranes, skin turgor, and ability to drink (especially in children)
findings.finding: Moist mucous membranes, normal skin turgor, drinking well

initial.test: Herpes simplex virus type-specific serology (HSV-1/HSV-2 IgG)
initial.why: Confirms prior HSV infection when the diagnosis is uncertain; not needed for a classic recurrent lip sore
initial.only_if: the diagnosis is unclear or the patient wants to know their HSV status

initial.why: Detects HSV from an unroofed vesicle when the diagnosis is in doubt
initial.only_if: the lesion is atypical, severe, or the patient is immunocompromised

confirmatory.test: HSV polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of lesion swab
confirmatory.why: Most sensitive and specific test to confirm HSV when the clinical picture is atypical or the diagnosis matters
confirmatory.only_if: atypical, severe, or recurrent lesions where confirmation changes management

supporting.why: Not routinely needed; may show a mild leukocytosis with a first episode or severe gingivostomatitis
supporting.only_if: severe first episode with fever or concern for a bacterial superinfection

supporting.why: Nonspecific; may be mildly elevated with a severe first episode
supporting.only_if: concern for bacterial superinfection or another inflammatory process

not_indicated.why: A classic recurrent cold sore is diagnosed clinically; blood counts do not change management
No role in an uncomplicated lip sore
Not needed for a typical cold sore
Not needed for a typical cold sore

not_indicated.test: Herpes simplex virus type-specific serology (HSV-1/HSV-2 IgG)
not_indicated.why: Does not distinguish a current outbreak from past infection and is not needed for a classic presentation
Not routine for a classic recurrent cold sore; yield falls as the lesion crusts

not_indicated.test: HSV polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of lesion swab
not_indicated.why: Not routine for a classic recurrent cold sore
Only if meningitis or encephalitis is suspected, which is not part of uncomplicated cold sores

not_indicated.test: MRI brain without and with contrast
not_indicated.why: Only if herpes encephalitis is suspected

decision_points: A classic recurrent vesicle at the lip margin is diagnosed clinically; testing is reserved for atypical, severe, or immunocompromised presentations
Consider referral or urgent evaluation if there is eye involvement, widespread skin lesions, or neurologic symptoms
In children, assess hydration and ability to drink; dehydration may require supportive care

differential.name: Herpetic whitlow
differential.why_considered: HSV infection of the finger can produce a painful vesicular lesion that may be mistaken for a cold sore when the patient reports a hand lesion or when the history is unclear.

history: Lesion on a finger or thumb, often after contact with a person who has a cold sore
Occupational exposure such as dental or health care work
No lip or perioral involvement
exam: Tense, painful vesicles on an erythematous base on the finger
Local tenderness and swelling of the digit
labs: HSV PCR of the lesion can confirm if needed

differential.name: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
differential.why_considered: A vesicular rash near the mouth or face could be confused with a cold sore, but zoster follows a dermatomal pattern and can involve the eye.
differential.trigger: Vesicles in a dermatomal distribution, especially near the eye or forehead, or any eye redness or pain

history: Pain or tingling in a band-like distribution before the rash
Rash on one side of the face, often forehead or cheek
Eye redness, pain, or blurred vision if the ophthalmic branch is involved
exam: Vesicles grouped in a dermatomal pattern that does not cross the midline
Conjunctival injection, corneal lesion, or decreased visual acuity if the eye is involved
labs: Varicella-zoster virus PCR of the lesion if the diagnosis is uncertain

differential.name: Aphthous ulcers (canker sores)
differential.why_considered: Painful mouth ulcers are a common complaint and can be mistaken for cold sores, especially when they occur inside the mouth.

history: Ulcers inside the mouth, often on the tongue, buccal mucosa, or soft palate
No tingling or burning before the ulcer appears
No vesicle stage; ulcers start as a round, shallow sore with a yellow-white center and red rim
Not contagious; no known viral trigger
exam: Single or few round, shallow ulcers with a gray-white base and erythematous halo

differential.name: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
differential.why_considered: Coxsackievirus infection can cause mouth sores and a rash, and in children it may present with fever and refusal to eat.

history: Fever, sore throat, and rash on hands and feet
Recent contact with a child with similar symptoms
Mouth sores are usually inside the mouth, not on the lip margin
exam: Vesicles or ulcers on the palms, soles, and sometimes buttocks
Mouth ulcers on the tongue, gums, and buccal mucosa
labs: Clinical diagnosis; viral PCR or serology rarely needed

differential.name: Herpangina
differential.why_considered: Another enteroviral illness that causes fever and painful mouth ulcers, often in children.

history: Sudden fever, sore throat, and refusal to eat
No lip tingling or cold sore history
exam: Small vesicles or ulcers on the soft palate, tonsils, and uvula

differential.name: Herpes simplex keratitis
differential.why_considered: HSV can infect the eye and cause a painful red eye with a dendritic corneal lesion; this can occur with or without a cold sore.
differential.trigger: Eye redness, pain, tearing, or blurred vision in a patient with a cold sore or recent HSV infection

history: Eye pain, redness, tearing, or photophobia
Blurred vision or foreign body sensation
May have a history of cold sores
exam: Conjunctival injection, corneal haze, or a dendritic ulcer on fluorescein staining
labs: HSV PCR of corneal scraping if needed, but usually clinical

differential.name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip
differential.why_considered: A non-healing lip lesion can be mistaken for a cold sore, especially if it persists beyond the typical 2 weeks.
differential.trigger: A lip sore that does not heal within 3 weeks, is indurated, or bleeds easily

history: Lesion present for weeks to months and progressively enlarging
No prodromal tingling or vesicle stage
History of sun exposure, smoking, or alcohol use
exam: Indurated, ulcerated, or crusted lesion on the lip that may be painless
May have palpable cervical lymph nodes
imaging: Biopsy is required for diagnosis; imaging of the neck may be considered if nodes are present

severity.mild: Prodromal tingling or a small cluster of vesicles at the lip margin; no fever, no systemic symptoms, able to eat and drink normally.
severity.moderate: Painful vesicles or ulcers with local tenderness, mild fever, tender submandibular lymph nodes, and discomfort with eating; no dehydration.
severity.severe: First episode with widespread oral ulcers (gingivostomatitis), fever, significant pain, difficulty eating or drinking, and possible mild dehydration; or recurrent outbreaks that are unusually large or frequent.
severity.critical: Disseminated HSV infection with widespread skin lesions, hepatitis, pneumonitis, or central nervous system involvement (encephalitis or meningitis); this is rare and occurs mainly in immunocompromised patients or neonates.

red_flags.finding: Eye redness, pain, or blurred vision
red_flags.meaning: Possible herpes simplex keratitis; urgent ophthalmology evaluation is needed to prevent corneal damage.

red_flags.finding: Severe headache, confusion, neck stiffness, or seizures
red_flags.meaning: Possible herpes encephalitis or meningitis; requires urgent evaluation and treatment.

red_flags.finding: Widespread vesicles beyond the lip or mouth, especially in an immunocompromised patient
red_flags.meaning: Possible disseminated HSV infection; needs urgent antiviral therapy.

red_flags.finding: Inability to drink, drooling, or signs of dehydration in a child
red_flags.meaning: Severe gingivostomatitis with dehydration; may require intravenous fluids and hospitalization.

red_flags.finding: Lip sore that does not heal within 3 weeks or is indurated and bleeding
red_flags.meaning: Possible squamous cell carcinoma; requires biopsy.

red_flags.finding: Neonate with fever, poor feeding, lethargy, or vesicles
red_flags.meaning: Possible neonatal HSV infection; a medical emergency requiring immediate evaluation and treatment.

complications.name: Herpes simplex keratitis
clues: Eye redness, pain, tearing, or blurred vision
Dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining

complications.name: Eczema herpeticum
clues: Widespread vesicular rash in a patient with atopic dermatitis

complications.name: Herpes encephalitis
clues: Fever, headache, confusion, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits
Abnormal cerebrospinal fluid with lymphocytic pleocytosis

complications.name: Dehydration from severe gingivostomatitis
clues: Inability to drink, drooling, decreased urine output

complications.name: Bacterial superinfection of the cold sore
clues: Increasing redness, swelling, pain, or purulent drainage

special_populations.differences: First episode often presents as gingivostomatitis with fever, irritability, swollen gums, multiple mouth ulcers, drooling, and refusal to eat. Assess hydration carefully; young children may need supportive care or hospitalization for fluids.

May present with fever, poor feeding, and irritability without a clear lip sore. Neonatal HSV infection can be severe and disseminated; any suspected neonatal infection requires urgent evaluation and treatment.

Sores may be larger, more numerous, slower to heal, and may spread to other skin areas or inside the mouth. Disseminated infection is more likely; antiviral therapy is often needed and may be given intravenously.

May have more frequent or slower-healing outbreaks. Other causes of mouth sores such as medication reactions, nutritional deficiencies, or malignancy are more likely and should be considered if the presentation is atypical.

Primary HSV infection near delivery can pose a risk of neonatal transmission. Recurrent cold sores are usually not dangerous, but pregnant patients should inform their obstetrician if they have active lesions at the time of labor.

key_questions.question: What does the sore look like, and where is it?
key_questions.looking_for: A cluster of small blisters or a crusted sore at the outer lip margin, corner of the mouth, or nostril

key_questions.question: Did you feel any tingling, itching, or burning before the sore appeared?
key_questions.looking_for: A prodrome of tingling or burning at the lip hours to a day before the blister — supports HSV

key_questions.question: How long has it been there, and is it getting better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Blister then crust then healing over 7–14 days; a sore that persists beyond 3 weeks is a red flag

key_questions.question: Have you had sores like this before?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent episodes at the same lip location — strongly supports recurrent herpes labialis

key_questions.question: What seems to bring them on?
key_questions.looking_for: Sun or wind exposure, stress, fatigue, fever or another illness, menstruation, dental work

key_questions.question: Does it hurt, and does it hurt to eat or drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Tenderness and burning; pain with eating suggests a first episode with mouth ulcers

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever or felt generally unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and malaise with a first episode (gingivostomatitis); usually absent in recurrences

key_questions.question: Any swollen or tender glands in the neck or under the jaw?
key_questions.looking_for: Tender submandibular or cervical nodes, more common with a first episode

key_questions.question: Any redness, pain, tearing, or blurred vision in your eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Eye involvement suggests herpes simplex keratitis and needs urgent ophthalmology evaluation

key_questions.question: Any severe headache, confusion, neck stiffness, or seizures?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests herpes encephalitis or meningitis — a medical emergency

key_questions.question: Do you have any condition or take any medicine that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression raises the risk of larger, slower-healing, or disseminated lesions

key_questions.question: Do you take any medicines by mouth or on the skin, including steroids or other immunosuppressants?
Do you have eczema or atopic dermatitis?
key_questions.looking_for: Atopic dermatitis raises the risk of eczema herpeticum if HSV spreads over the skin

key_questions.question: Has anyone close to you had a cold sore, and do you share drinks, utensils, or lip balm?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent contact with an active cold sore; sharing items that touch the mouth

key_questions.question: Do you have any genital sores or blisters?
key_questions.looking_for: Genital lesions suggest HSV-2 or genital herpes rather than a simple cold sore

key_questions.question: Any widespread rash, blisters elsewhere on the body, or skin peeling?
key_questions.looking_for: Widespread vesicles suggest disseminated HSV or another diagnosis such as eczema herpeticum

key_questions.question: Any unintentional weight loss, night sweats, or a sore that bleeds easily?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms or a non-healing, indurated, bleeding lip lesion raise concern for malignancy

reasoning_points: Recurrent episodes of a small cluster of vesicles at the outer lip margin or nostril
A prodrome of tingling, itching, or burning at the lip before the blister appears
The lesion progresses from vesicles to crusting and heals without a scar in about 1–2 weeks
Triggers such as sun or wind exposure, stress, fever, or menstruation
Typical lesions are diagnosed clinically; testing is reserved for atypical, severe, or immunocompromised presentations
Red flags such as eye involvement, neurologic symptoms, widespread lesions, dehydration, or a sore that has not healed in 3 weeks are absent
Look-alikes such as aphthous ulcers, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, herpes zoster, and squamous cell carcinoma of the lip are considered and excluded

easy: Young adult with a recurrent tingling blister at the lip margin
Clear prodrome followed by a cluster of vesicles that crusts and heals
Known triggers such as sun exposure or stress
No fever, no eye symptoms, no systemic illness
medium: First episode in a child with fever, swollen gums, multiple mouth ulcers, and refusal to eat
Lesion at the corner of the mouth or nostril rather than the mid-lip
Patient with atopic dermatitis and a few vesicles spreading onto the cheek
Older adult with a slower-healing outbreak and other possible causes of mouth sores
hard: Immunocompromised patient with large, numerous, or slowly healing lesions
Neonate or infant with fever, poor feeding, and irritability without a clear lip sore
Lip lesion that has not healed in 3 weeks or is indurated and bleeding
Patient with eye redness, pain, or blurred vision suggesting herpetic keratitis
Severe gingivostomatitis with dehydration requiring supportive care
